title: Anticoagulation forgotten
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in orthopaedics. Mr Day, 70, who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, had a hip replacement two days ago. The plan was to restart his apixaban the day after surgery.

You were responsible for restarting it, but forgot. A pharmacist notices 36 hours late.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Check Mr Day for clots or stroke, and restart his apixaban.
options.detailed: Missing anticoagulation raises his risk of stroke and clots. Checking him and restarting it promptly reduces the risk.

options.text: Restart it, and record that it was paused intentionally.
options.detailed: This hides your error and is dishonest. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Report the missed doses through the trust's incident reporting system.
options.detailed: Reporting helps the team prevent similar errors. It ranks fourth because it's less urgent.

options.text: Explain to Mr Day what happened, and apologise.
options.brief: He has a right to know.
options.detailed: Being open with him about the missed doses and apologising is part of your professional duty of candour. It ranks third because his safety and your senior come first.
Your registrar should know, so they can make sure his care is right and support you.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you put a patient's safety first after your own error, and are open about it.
explanation.keyDetails: Apixaban was missed for 36 hours. He has atrial fibrillation and has had surgery. It was your responsibility.
explanation.reasoning: [A] protects him, [E] informs your senior, [D] is open with him, and [C] supports learning. [B] falsifies the record.
explanation.competing: Some would tell Mr Day before the registrar. Either is reasonable; the key puts the registrar first because they may need to review him.

references.title: Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour
references.publisher: General Medical Council and Nursing and Midwifery Council
references.note: Being open with patients when something goes wrong.
